account: The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) page “How we use data and analytics” states that the ATO uses machine learning, a common form of artificial intelligence. Nearest neighbor methods compare amounts being entered into myTax with those of other people in similar circumstances. If a claim is significantly different from what is expected, a message prompts the taxpayer to check the figures. During tax time in 2020 nearly 340,000 taxpayers, around 7.5% of myTax users, received a pop-up message, the page reports. It suggested they review a specific label. These prompts caused taxpayers to make adjustments estimated to have a revenue impact of around $37 million. The same page says the ATO also uses machine-learning algorithms to forecast call-center volumes and speech recognition to transcribe inbound calls. Separately, in 2020 it automated 93,000 franking-credit refunds worth over $42 million for self-preparers over 60 (not described as machine learning). The only cited source independent of the ATO is The Mandarin's report of 25 February 2025. It says the Australian National Audit Office (ANAO) found the ATO's AI governance arrangements only partly effective, and gives no outcome figures. No non-vendor primary source on record gives a recovered figure attributable to machine learning. The $37 million is the ATO's own estimate. The page is undated; the outcome concerns tax time 2020. An Internet Archive copy dated 14 July 2021 contains the 340,000 and $37 million figures.

ai_role.statement: The ATO page states that nearest-neighbor methods generate the prompts and that the ATO uses machine learning. It attributes the adjustments to the prompts, though taxpayers themselves make the changes. Only the deployer's account is among the sources for the outcome. The ATO built and runs the system in-house, so its page is both the developer's and the deployer's account. The ANAO audit reported by The Mandarin found AI governance “partly effective” and offers no outcome figures in the cited excerpt.

fields.account: The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) page “How we use data and analytics” states that the ATO uses machine learning, a common form of artificial intelligence. Nearest neighbor methods compare amounts being entered into myTax with those of other people in similar circumstances. If a claim is significantly different from what is expected, a message prompts the taxpayer to check the figures. During tax time in 2020 nearly 340,000 taxpayers, around 7.5% of myTax users, received a pop-up message, the page reports. It suggested they review a specific label. These prompts caused taxpayers to make adjustments estimated to have a revenue impact of around $37 million. The same page says the ATO also uses machine-learning algorithms to forecast call-center volumes and speech recognition to transcribe inbound calls. Separately, in 2020 it automated 93,000 franking-credit refunds worth over $42 million for self-preparers over 60 (not described as machine learning). The only cited source independent of the ATO is The Mandarin's report of 25 February 2025. It says the Australian National Audit Office (ANAO) found the ATO's AI governance arrangements only partly effective, and gives no outcome figures. No non-vendor primary source on record gives a recovered figure attributable to machine learning. The $37 million is the ATO's own estimate. The page is undated; the outcome concerns tax time 2020. An Internet Archive copy dated 14 July 2021 contains the 340,000 and $37 million figures.

fields.account: The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) page “How we use data and analytics” states that the ATO uses machine learning, a common form of artificial intelligence. Nearest neighbor methods compare amounts being entered into myTax with those of other people in similar circumstances. If a claim is significantly different from what is expected, a message prompts the taxpayer to check the figures. During tax time in 2020 nearly 340,000 taxpayers, around 7.5% of myTax users, received a pop-up message, the page reports. It suggested they review a specific label. These prompts caused taxpayers to make adjustments estimated to have a revenue impact of around $37 million. The same page says the ATO also uses machine-learning algorithms to forecast call-center volumes and speech recognition to transcribe inbound calls. Separately, in 2020 it automated 93,000 franking-credit refunds worth over $42 million for self-preparers over 60 (not described as machine learning). The only cited source independent of the ATO is The Mandarin's report of 25 February 2025. It says the Australian National Audit Office (ANAO) found the ATO's AI governance arrangements only partly effective, and gives no outcome figures. No non-vendor primary source on record gives a recovered figure attributable to machine learning. The $37 million is the ATO's own estimate. The page is undated; the outcome concerns tax time 2020. An Internet Archive copy dated 14 July 2021 contains the 340,000 and $37 million figures.

purpose: Built to prompt myTax users in real time to check claims that differ from those of similar taxpayers before lodgment. The recorded adjustments are that purpose.

ratings.reason: Taxpayers who corrected claims are not individually documented; the page gives no individual outcome beyond the aggregate prompt count.
The ATO's own estimate of about $37 million revenue impact from one tax time, with no independent verification and no comparison with total collections given.
Protects public revenue at modest scale: prompts reached 7.5% of myTax users and the stated impact is an estimate.
